findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for, and what problem it solves, in plain words. A newcomer can say what this is after one paragraph.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: This is Athena's home URL, but the title and headline are about a different project, firstmate. A newcomer may not be sure whether the page is about Athena or firstmate until they read the three lede paragraphs.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title> / h1 of the same text

findings.text: What to do next is clear and concrete: a link near the top jumps to prerequisites, clone, install and a first command. A newcomer can act on it.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section: "git clone https://github.com/doodla/athena.git", "./setup.sh", "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The page promises cost records, a second model checking the work, and a verdict, but the study shows none of these: no cost, no models, no verdict for this study. So the 'why it matters' claim is stated but never demonstrated.
findings.source: Lede: "records what each step cost" and "a commit they can trace to the request, the models, the cost and the verdict"

findings.text: Most of the page is a dense state machine of firstmate, with exit codes, locks and pending-close records. A newcomer who wants to understand Athena gets little from it beyond 'Athena can produce this', and may give up scrolling.
findings.source: Sections "States of a piece of work", "Counters", "Transitions" (t1–t12), "Claims and sources" (c1–c45)

findings.text: This link speaks to the project owner, not a visitor, and sits in the header next to the newcomer's next step. A newcomer will not know what 'proposals' or 'your decision' means here.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Several glossary entries say the term is undefined in the source. This is honest, but it leaves the newcomer with words they cannot understand in the firstmate explanation.
findings.source: Glossary: "captain call — The firstmate source does not define a captain call." Similar entries for durable record, endpoint, heartbeat, wake

findings.text: These notes about how the study was made and where it is stored are internal details. They mean nothing to a first-time visitor and make the page feel unfinished.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f3: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths..."; About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/"

findings.text: The 'Start here' section and the 'Words used first' list are well ordered for a reader who does want to learn firstmate: terms are defined before use and every statement links to source lines.
findings.source: Start here: "The three parts below say what firstmate is, follow one piece of work, and say what happens when something fails"
